title: Did Early Humans Keep Souvenirs 500,000 Years Ago?
paragraphs: Most of us keep souvenirs: a shell from a holiday, a ticket from a concert. A new paper suggests that the habit of keeping such objects may be extremely old, perhaps about half a million years.

The paper, published in the journal Evolutionary Anthropology, comes from researchers at Tel Aviv University and Oxford University. They point to evidence from sites in Israel. At Qesem Cave, people carried in small, colourful pebbles from other places, and no practical use for them has been found. Older flint tools that had weathered were also kept, with their original surface left in place. In the Sakhnin Valley, handaxes were made from flint that contained fossils, and those features were kept in the middle of the stone.

The team argues that such objects worked like an outside memory aid, helping people recall places and experiences. However, the authors describe this as a hypothesis. They do not claim that every unusual stone was a keepsake, and nobody can be sure what these early people were thinking.

questions.q: What kind of objects were found at Qesem Cave?
questions.a: Small, colourful pebbles brought from other places.

questions.q: How could such objects have helped people?
questions.a: They may have worked like an outside memory aid for places and experiences.

questions.q: How do the authors describe their claim?
questions.a: As a hypothesis, not as proof.
